[MATH: \displaystyle\int_{\color{blue}a}^{\color{blue}a} f(x) \, \textrm d x = 0.]

Example Prompt:
Given that [MATH: {\displaystyle \int_{0}^{6} \, f(x) \; \textrm d x = -54 },] what is the value of
[MATH: {\displaystyle \int_{6}^{0} \bigg( \dfrac 1 3 f(x) + 1 \bigg) \; \textrm d x }?]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Let's reverse the limits of integration on the known result:
[MATH: ∫_{6}^{0}f(x)dx = − ∫_{0}^{6}f(x)dx = 54]

Now, we can split up the given integral using the sum rule and factor out the constants. We get

[MATH: ∫_{6}^{0}((1)/(3)f(x) + 1)dx|= (1)/(3)∫_{6}^{0}f(x)dx + ∫_{6}^{0}1dx; = (1)/(3) ⋅ 54 + x|_{6}^{0}; = 18 + (0 − 6); = 12.]

Item 9 — Tutorial: The Integral of a Function Over Adjacent Intervals

Content:
The last property states that if we have the sum of two integrals with the same integrand, and where the lower bound of one integral matches the upper bound of the other integral, such as
[MATH: \displaystyle \int_{-3}^{\color{blue}0} 4x^2\, \textrm d x + \int_{\color{blue}0}^{5} 4x^2\, \textrm d x,]
then we can combine the two integrals into a single integral as follows:
[MATH: \int_{-3}^{\color{blue}0} 4x^2\, \textrm d x + \int_{\color{blue}0}^{5} 4x^2\, \textrm d x = \int_{-3}^{5} 4x^2\, \textrm d x]

Content:
In general,
[MATH: \int_a^c f(x) \, \textrm d x + \int_c^b f(x) \, \textrm d x = \int_a^b f(x)\, \textrm d x.]

Content:
To understand the reasoning behind this rule, remember that the integrals represent area. So, the rule states that the area bounded by a function on the interval [MATH: [a,b]] is equal to the sum of areas on the adjacent intervals [MATH: [a,c]] and [MATH: [c,b].]

Item 10 — Example: Evaluating a Definite Integral Given Integrals Over Adjacent Intervals

Example Prompt:
If [MATH: \displaystyle \int_7^{10}f(x)\,\textrm d x = 18] and [MATH: \displaystyle \int_0^{7}f(x)\,\textrm d x = -6] then what is [MATH: \displaystyle \int_0^{10} \big( 2f(x)+1 \big) \,\textrm d x?]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
From the adjacent intervals rule, we know that

[MATH: \int_0^{7}f(x)\,\textrm d x + \displaystyle \int_7^{10}f(x)\,\textrm d x = \displaystyle \int_0^{10}f(x)\,\textrm d x.]

Plugging in the known information into the above gives the following:

[MATH: − 6 + 18 = ∫_{0}^{10}f(x)dx; 12 = ∫_{0}^{10}f(x)dx]

Finally, we compute the desired integral and get

[MATH: ∫_{0}^{10}(2f(x) + 1)dx|= 2∫_{0}^{10}f(x)dx + ∫_{0}^{10}dx; = 2(12) + x|_{0}^{10}; = 24 + (10 − 0); = 34.]

[MATH: ∫_{4}^{1}2f(x)dx|= − 1; 2∫_{4}^{1}f(x)dx|= − 1; − 2∫_{1}^{4}f(x)dx|= − 1; ∫_{1}^{4}f(x)dx|= (1)/(2).]
The second integral can be rewritten as follows:
[MATH: ∫_{1}^{− 1}f(x)dx|= 2; − ∫_{− 1}^{1}f(x)dx|= 2; ∫_{− 1}^{1}f(x)dx|= − 2.]

Then, from the adjacent intervals rule, we get
[MATH: ∫_{− 1}^{4}f(x)dx|= ∫_{− 1}^{1}f(x)dx + ∫_{1}^{4}f(x)dx; = − 2 + (1)/(2); = − (3)/(2).]
